newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Hurricane kills 10 in Central America, Cuba braces.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane kills 10 in Central America, Cuba braces.

text.p: At least 10 people were killed in Central America and hundreds driven from their homes by torrential rain from Hurricane Lili, which appeared set to unleash its full force across Cuba on Thursday.
The highest death toll was in Nicaragua, where Civil Defence officials said five people drowned in swollen rivers in different parts of the country over the past four days.

In neighbouring Costa Rica, officials said four people died and the country's coffee crop had likely suffered damage. In Honduras a boy was killed when his Tegucigalpa shantytown house collapsed. Hundreds were left homeless.
"Tropical Storm Lili caused extensive flooding in parts of northern Nicaragua, and five people drowned in the swollen waters," Nicaraguan Civil Defence Capt. Javier Gadea told Reuters.

Hundreds of people in Nicaragua's northern deparments of Esteli and Jinotega were forced to flee to high ground as swollen rivers flooded their homes and civil defence authorities are worried about the threat of mudslides.
In Cuba, authorities were bracing for the full onslaught of Hurricane Lili, which began early in the week as a depression, and had already started to evacute people from Havana.
Cuba's Civil Defence organisation has ordered a hurricane emergency in central provinces as well as the western areas of the country, including the capital.
Forecasters said Hurricane Lili was expected to hit southwestern areas of the island at around midnight Thursday (0500 GMT Friday).

A tropical storm warning and hurricane watch remained in effect for the Cayman Islands. Forecasters said alerts could be issued for the Florida Keys and parts of the Bahamas later on Thursday. U.S. forecasters warned boaters in the Florida Keys to remain in port.
U.S. National Hurricane Centre forecasters in Miami said the forward motion of the storm, a minimal hurricane with winds of 75 mph (120 kph), could slow in the next 24 hours.

At 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT), the centre of Lili was located at latitude 20.4 north, longitude 83.1 west, about 185 miles (300 km) south-southwest of Havana, and was moving to the north-northeast at about 9 mph (15 kph).

Hurricane-force winds extended 25 miles (40 km) from the centre and tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 140 miles (220 km). Rainfall up to 12 inches (30 cm) was likely over Cuba and the Cayman Islands and storm surge flooding of three to six feet (1-2 metres) was possible near where the storm crosses mainland Cuba, forecasters said.

Cuba, slowly emerging from the worst of an economic crisis caused by the collapse of the former Soviet Union, could be badly hurt by the hurricane. At this time of year the key sugar cane crop, a crucial source of foreign exchange, is just two or three months away from being harvested.

Civil Defence spokesman Heriberto Diaz Perez told state television that by midday 28,000 people had been evacuated from their homes. Many were from parts of Havana where houses are in poor condition and in danger of collapsing and officials said as many as 62,000 people may have to move.
The state news agency AIN reported 31 partial house collapses in Havana in the past two days due to heavy rain -- a sign of the vulnerability of many buildings in the capital.
Some 325 foreign tourists were evacuated to the mainland from Cayo Lago, a small holiday island to the south of Cuba.
And 82,000 high school students at boarding schools in the countryside were returned home. Schools in the capital were closed, as were many workplaces.
In the countryside, some 130,000 heads of livestock and chickens were moved to safer places.

Provinces under hurricane emergency were Pinar del Rio, Matanzas, Havana, the Isle of Youth, Cienfuegos, Villa Clara, Sancti Spiritus and Ciego de Avila and people were urged to secure their homes, lay in stocks of drinking water and food and help clear debris from the streets.
Cuban weather forecaster Jose Rubiera said the hurricane looked likely hit land along the southern coast of Matanzas province, moving north out to sea on Friday morning.

Florida officials were continuing to watch the hurricane's path before deciding if evacuations were necessary. "We are in stand-by mode right now," said Monroe County Sheriff's Office spokesman Greg Artman. "We've told people to prepare but there are no orders for an evacuation as yet."
